Include the AI session logs that cover your work when you submit. Switches model or reasoning level for the task at hand, in whichever agent they use, and states the reason: cost, speed or difficulty. Handles customer data and untrusted input on purpose - redacting personal data, keeping it out of prompts and logs, guarding AI steps against injected instructions - and raises a risk specific to this customer's data that the agent did not. Tighten the guardrails / tool-access / done-definition for a regulated (6103 / ATO'd) repo beyond the general M7 default; propose an agent-in-PR autonomy boundary; require Cyber sign-off (does NOT make the compliance determination). Agnostic substrate: partition context physically by distribution rights (sidecar segmentation — redacted main committable, sensitive segment terminal); near-zero residual-risk tolerance — probabilistic mitigation is categorically insufficient ('99% is a failing grade'), so ensure the agent never holds the full lethal trifecta over protected data and cut the cheapest leg (exfiltration — no network reach to taxpayer data); conditional autonomy gated on a safety backstop existing (refuse if unguarded). The federal specifics (6103 data isolation, ATO sign-off gate, approved-tools-only, agent-in-PR boundary) are net-new TO52 overlay from PROGRAM docs, applied on top — no studied source addresses 6103 / ATO / FedRAMP / FISMA directly. Graded on the tightened settings + proposed boundary + required-sign-off note. Worked example (swappable): Codex tightened sandbox / approval; the federal acts come from program context. Take a recognized constraint and work out concretely what it requires THIS task to do: classify the protected surface (which specific fields are §6103-protected, which action is a regulated write, which hop crosses a confidentiality boundary), name what the classification triggers in plain delivery terms (e.g. §6103 -> masking + access logging + restricted scope; ATO -> control map + POA&M; non-FedRAMP dependency -> authorized-service substitution; AI step in a taxpayer-data repo -> guardrail + approval-policy tightening; Section-508 surface -> keyboard/screen-reader pass), state the forbidden actions, write it up as an actionable delivery requirement, and route it to the owning domain. Distinct from F1 (recognize/name/point only) — D1 grades the it-applies-HERE classification + the concrete trigger + the actionable hand-off. Does NOT build the control. LLM native “function calling” lets a large language model decide when to run a piece of code and which inputs to pass to it. You first tell the model what functions are available. For each one you give a short name, a short description, and a list of arguments with their types. During a chat, the model can answer in JSON that matches this schema instead of plain text. Your wrapper program reads the JSON, calls the real function, and then feeds the result back to the model so it can keep going. This loop helps an agent search the web, look up data, send an email, or do any other task you expose. Because the output is structured, you get fewer mistakes than when the model tries to write raw code or natural-language commands. In Git, a remote is a reference to a repository that exists on another server or system. Remotes allow you to access and interact with a copy of your repository that is stored elsewhere, making it possible to collaborate with others, share your work, and maintain multiple copies of your repository for backup and disaster recovery purposes. When you add a remote to your local repository, Git creates a reference to the remote repository, enabling you to push changes from your local repository to the remote one, pull changes from the remote to your local one, or fetch changes from the remote without updating your local copy. This enables distributed development and helps maintain a centralized version of your project's history, making it easier to track changes, manage conflicts, and ensure that everyone has access to the most up-to-date code. Viewing diffs in Git is crucial for understanding the changes made to your code. This is especially important when collaborating with others or reviewing your own work over time. Diffs show you exactly what lines have been added, modified, or removed between different versions of your files. This feature helps in code review processes, troubleshooting issues, and maintaining a clear history of your project's evolution. Git provides various commands and tools to view these differences, making it easier to track and manage changes effectively. Branches in Git serve as separate lines of development that allow multiple features or changes to be worked on simultaneously without affecting the main codebase. With branches, you can create isolated environments for different tasks, collaborate with others, and manage complex workflows. Collaboration on GitHub is a powerful way for multiple people to work together on the same project, using Git as the version control system. GitHub provides various tools and workflows that make collaboration efficient and organized. Measure whether a harness change (a rule, a skill, a context move, an added agent) actually helps: design an eval on a real task with paired with / without arms in the same turn (control for run-to-run drift); a concrete machine-checkable threshold for 'done'; flag variance / flakiness; grade objective things by assertion + subjective things by judgment; never fabricate a baseline with nothing to subtract from; for a guardrail, an adaptive-adversary eval (the attacker tunes against the defense). Evaluation is the gate that licenses added architecture; failure observation drives the tool / interface fix (the observed failure is the spec for the fix). Graded on an eval design + the measured lift + an honest scope-limit statement. Worked example (swappable): run a Codex task with / without a rules or skill change on the same ticket and score the diff + a done.sh threshold; eval-runner flags -> appendix. Read the code the harness produced; judge it for clarity (is this more complex than the job needs, is there duplication that should collapse, are names/structure readable); direct the AI to cut complexity and remove duplication; decide when it is simple and maintainable enough to ship and own — rather than shipping the first version that runs. 'Working' is the harness's proof; 'maintainable' is the human's call, because only the person who will read and change it can judge whether it is clean enough to own, a judgment that needs the requirement and who maintains it next. Closed boundary: not correctness, not coverage/gates, not per-service acceptance. Backend Testing is a testing method that checks the server side or database of web applications or software. Backend testing aims to test the application layer or database layer to ensure that the web application or software is free from database defects like deadlock, data corruption, or data loss.

result.output:
# AI Full Stack Challenge — IT Access Requests

I got everything done by not challenging Codex. I said yes to everything it wanted.

## Setup and reproducible mock intake

Run from the repository root on Linux with CPython 3.11 or later. Implementation
checks were run on Python 3.12.3. No third-party dependencies are required;
requirements.lock records that dependency set. The validator implements the
type, properties, required, additionalProperties, enum and items vocabulary of
the supplied snapshot.schema.json, plus date and supporting-quote checks.

```bash
python3 --version
env -u API_KEY python3 -m access_requests intake materials/requests materials/synthetic
env -u API_KEY python3 -m access_requests queue
env -u API_KEY python3 -m access_requests accuracy --report deliverables/accuracy.md
env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

Default mode uses saved responses in tests/mock_responses/, labelled mock with
model fixture-v1. It never reads API_KEY or contacts a model. Mock fixtures do
not establish actual model extraction accuracy. Twenty original exports and one
authored paraphrase produce 21 records; expected facts, quotes and routing rules
are in planning/plan.md and tests/expected.json, independently of measured outputs.

Intake accepts files or directories of UTF-8 JSON exports. New messages in the
same export format are supported by the provider adapter; mock mode requires a
matching lowercase filename in the fixture directory. Missing mock fixtures
become explicit errors, not synthetic successes.

## Inspect and recover

An intake command can run in one terminal while another inspects the same state:

```bash
python3 -m access_requests queue
python3 -m access_requests history IT-001.json
python3 -m access_requests resume
python3 -m access_requests retry IT-001.json
python3 -m access_requests export
```

Queue output includes completed/error current records and a separate pending
list. All successes await human review. A manager is a contact, not an approval.
Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system
owner for a decision; the application never grants access or approves requests.

SQLite at state/requests.db is authoritative. Current output snapshots are
deliverables/extractions.jsonl and deliverables/queue.json, linked by document_id,
source_sha256 and attempt_id. `export` publishes both from one database snapshot.
Each is a symlink through deliverables/current to one immutable generation;
resolve current once before opening both files if publication may occur between
reads. Prior attempts are separate in SQLite, available through `history`, and
included in deliverables/history.jsonl. Source bytes, settings and policy version
are retained in the database. Completed results are reused only when source and
relevant processing inputs are unchanged. Batch omissions do not withdraw records.

`intake`, `resume` and `retry` publish snapshots when the command finishes. During
intake use `queue` to inspect ready work, or run `export` for a partial snapshot.
Existing committed snapshots can be inspected without a database; generate a new
local database with intake before using the database-backed queue command.

Every terminal extraction error includes an explicit retry_command with its
database, document and attempt. For an isolated workspace, put global flags before
the command, for example:

```bash
python3 -m access_requests --db /tmp/northstar.db --output /tmp/northstar-results intake materials/requests materials/synthetic
python3 -m access_requests --db /tmp/northstar.db queue
python3 -m access_requests --db /tmp/northstar.db retry IT-001.json --attempt 1
```

An explicit retry creates a new attempt, even after success. Failed retries show
the latest error, with earlier successes only in history. Retry retains the
chosen attempt's source bytes and policy; use the original provider/model
settings shown in history. Resuming requires those settings too. During a delayed
transient retry the document is pending; earlier failed attempts remain in history.

## Provider and configuration

The implemented live integration uses the OpenAI Responses API, direct JSON over
HTTPS and strict structured output. The documented configuration is
gpt-4.1-2025-04-14, temperature 0, max_output_tokens 2500, timeout 30 seconds and
store false. The facilitator supplies API_KEY in the environment; the application
reads it only when the openai provider is selected. Tests inject a dummy credential
directly and intercept transport, without reading API_KEY or contacting a model.
See docs/provider.md and deliverables/request-evidence.json for the contract and
credential-redacted request example. No live observation has been made.

For an optional operator-run provider intake, with the supplied environment set:

```bash
python3 -m access_requests --provider openai --db state/live.db --output state/live-results --rate 1 intake materials/requests
```

| Setting | Default and purpose |
|---|---|
| API_KEY | Required only for live provider authentication; never stored in settings or request evidence |
| MODEL_ID | gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 |
| MODEL_ENDPOINT | https://api.openai.com/v1/responses |
| MODEL_TEMPERATURE | 0 |
| MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS | 2500 |
| MODEL_TIMEOUT | 30 seconds |
| --db / --output | state/requests.db / deliverables |
| --provider / --fixtures | mock / tests/mock_responses/ |
| --workers / --rate | 4 concurrent workers / unlimited starts per second; rate is per process |
| --retries / --backoff | 2 transient retries / 1-second exponential base delay |
| --lease | 60 seconds, renewed every third of a lease while a call runs |
| --policy | Supplied materials/office-policy.md text by default; its SHA-256 identifies the policy version |
| --script | Optional comma-separated saved mock replies for reproducible error/retry examples |

Relevant model/request settings, prompt, schema, policy and raw-byte source hash
determine refresh. Logging verbosity and scheduling limits do not affect extracted
facts. Routing rules are implemented in policy.py; when policy semantics change,
update and test that implementation alongside policy text, then rerun intake on
affected documents. Unsupported policy hashes are rejected before registration;
update the supported hash only after implementing and testing the new rules.
Arbitrary new routing rules are not interpreted from prose.
Provider HTTP diagnostics are not recorded; errors use redacted summaries.

## Operating limits and verification

Shared operation supports overlapping processes on a single host using one local
SQLite database. It does not support network filesystems or independent regional
databases. Latest intake registration order determines the current source revision;
export timestamps do not order business updates. An obsolete worker is fenced from
changing the current result. A killed worker's claim can be recovered after its
lease expires; completed work remains recorded. If a process dies after a provider
returns but before a result commits, the call may run again: model calls are at
least once, with one coherent current record per document.

Workers and call rates are bounded per process, not globally across operators or
other internal tools. Use a suitable shared provider quota and lower --rate when
needed. Model calls have configurable timeouts and bounded transient retries.
Filesystem publication requires Linux flock, symlinks, atomic rename and fsync.
Generations are retained; disk usage grows and cleanup is an operator task.

Verification commands, comparisons, observed mock results, interruption behavior
and limits are recorded in deliverables/verification.md. The accuracy command is
for the supplied benchmark and paraphrase, not an evaluation of arbitrary intake
messages. It counts all 252 scalar opportunities, even when extraction fails or a
record is missing. Alternate purpose paraphrases need human source review.

The coding session is captured by the repository's enabled Entire setup and its
commit hooks. Final facilitator capture verification, a default-branch push and
Classroom root-link submission require actual external evidence; local tests do
not prove those actions occurred. Human validation of every spec line remains
the reviewer's decision.

Run the offline artifact inventory with:

```bash
python3 -m access_requests readiness https://github.com/JagdeepSSandhu/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests
```

See deliverables/submission.md for capture evidence and remaining external checks.

result.output:
# AI Full Stack Challenge — IT Access Requests

## The task
Northstar Labs receives access requests as free-text messages. Build a small runnable application that uses a language model to turn those messages into structured records and a review queue for the IT team. The supplied company, people and requests are fictional.

Read docs/requirements.md for the operating context and required behavior, materials/office-policy.md for review rules, and snapshot.schema.json for the record format. The 20 JSON exports in materials/requests/ are your starting data. Choose an interface suited to the IT team: a CLI, service or web application. Operators should be able to start intake, inspect completed results while other requests are pending, and resume unfinished work through the documented interface.

## What to submit
This brief ships as CHALLENGE.md; the README.md below is yours to write.

| Path | Content |
|---|---|
| README.md | Setup, supported runtime/provider, exact intake/test/accuracy-check commands, environment-variable names, and how to inspect the queue |
| Source code and dependency lockfile | Runnable application, extraction prompt, schema and model request configuration |
| deliverables/extractions.jsonl | One current record per message: document_id, source_sha256, extraction (schema-conforming object, or null on error), status, owner, next_action, error (null on success), and response_source (`mock`, or the provider and model ID that produced the record) |
| deliverables/queue.json | The review queue linked to extraction records by document_id |
| deliverables/accuracy.md | Source-derived expected fields for the 20 supplied messages and one paraphrase you author; the field-comparison procedure, exact-match counting/denominator rules, factual-error reporting and model/configuration; distinguish mocked examples from any optional live observations |
| deliverables/request-evidence.json | Credential-redacted example model request showing the model ID and configuration used, plus the implemented response handling |
| deliverables/verification.md | Verification commands and assertions, their intended comparisons, operating limits, and any observed results or repairs clearly identified as such |
| Coding-session capture | Session record paired with the submitted commit, collected through the facilitator's capture setup |

## Submission
Commit and push the application, outputs and session capture to your repository's default branch. Submit only the root repository link (`https://github.com/<your-account>/<repository>`) through the Classroom assignment. The facilitator supplies the assignment and capture instructions.

Submit the implemented provider integration and source-grounded validation procedure. Use mocked responses for reproducible development examples, and label each recorded observation with its configuration and whether it used a mock or provider response. The committed deliverables may come from mocked or provider responses; each record's response_source says which.
# Submission handoff

Offline readiness command:

```bash
python3 -m access_requests readiness https://github.com/JagdeepSSandhu/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests
```

The inventory checks nonempty required files and the root-link shape. It does not
validate source correctness, capture integrity, remote state or Classroom state.

The enabled Entire capture setup is tracked in .entire/settings.json and
.codex/hooks.json. The session snapshot is deliverables/session.jsonl; metadata,
its SHA-256 and the commit present at snapshot time are in session-capture.json.
The snapshot is bounded to the transcript available when exported. Each build
commit's automatic Entire-Checkpoint footer links the continuing session; no
manual checkpoint was created. A final commit cannot embed its own hash inside
an artifact that contributes to that hash.

Final external checks remain pending:

1. Compare the final commit's Entire-Checkpoint and session pairing with the
   facilitator's capture instructions (C-05). Locally inspect `git log -1
   --format=%B`, `entire status --json` and the documented read-only session info.
2. Confirm the intended default branch and push the application, outputs and
   capture through the authorized submission workflow; inspect remote contents
   afterwards (C-06).
3. Submit only the root repository link above to the Classroom assignment and
   inspect that actual submission (C-07).

No remote push or Classroom submission is asserted by this handoff. Human
validation of each spec line is also separate from a passing automated suite.
# Verification commands and evidence

All observations below used mock responses and configuration provider=mock,
model=fixture-v1, unless explicitly described as an intercepted provider contract.
They are pipeline checks, not live extraction-quality measurements. No real model
was called and tests do not read API_KEY. Runtime observed: Python 3.12.3 on Linux.

## Commands and intended comparisons

```bash
env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
env -u API_KEY python3 -m access_requests intake materials/requests materials/synthetic
env -u API_KEY python3 -m access_requests queue
env -u API_KEY python3 -m access_requests accuracy --report deliverables/accuracy.md
```

Use --db and --output global flags for an isolated workspace as in README.md.
The final suite runs T-01–T-40 plus three preserved starter checks.
planning/test-run.txt records the actual whole-suite run. T-40 checks nonempty
required artifacts and root-link shape, not external submission completion.

| Cases | Intended assertions/comparisons |
|---|---|
| T-01–T-04 | Saved mock events, original-byte hashes, filenames, decoded quote substrings, schema/dates, metadata isolation and 200-word input |
| T-05–T-20 | Expected E01–E21 facts authored in planning/plan.md, ordered policy routes, missing/conflicting/corrected facts and instruction overrides |
| T-21–T-25 | Malformed, refused, incomplete and failed responses do not yield successful extractions; HTTP contract model/settings and redaction match saved protocol fixtures |
| T-26–T-31 | Current/history separation, reuse, changed source, failed retries, batch omission and settings/policy provenance |
| T-32 | Two processes leave one coherent current entry per document; a stale worker cannot replace a new source; process death before generation switch leaves old output readable |
| T-33–T-36 | Slow work does not hide completed work; killed workers resume; transient retries preserve attempts; 400- and 2,000-message mock batches are accounted for |
| T-37–T-39 | Real CLI commands operate offline in isolated workspaces; independent comparison detects mutated facts, errors and missing records; handover artifacts match documented configuration |

## Observed mock results

The final whole-suite run passed all 43 tests in 51.727 seconds. Its T-36 mock
workload observations were 4.605 seconds for 400 messages and 32.043 seconds for

# Requirements — IT Access Requests

## Operating context

Northstar Labs is a fictional multinational company with approximately 5,000 employees across offices in Asia, Europe and North America. Its regional IT teams share responsibility for preparing access requests for human review. They receive free-text messages through email, chat and the service portal, then work from JSON exports of those messages.

### Workload and the review day

On an ordinary business day, the company receives around 200–400 request messages. A coordinated onboarding or acquisition can bring roughly 2,000 messages into the morning's intake. The supplied 20 exports are a representative sample of message types; the application will also receive other messages in the same export format.

Reviewers begin work at different local times. They want to start on requests that are ready while the rest of the intake is still being prepared. A slow response for one message should leave the rest of their work available. Model access is shared with other internal tools, and the available request rate and response time can vary.

### Shared operations

Regional operators work against the same intake and review records. Their working hours overlap, and two operators may start processing around the same time. Each expects their work to leave a coherent current queue and a trustworthy record of earlier activity.

The application may be stopped during a deployment or interrupted by a service outage. When an operator returns, they need to distinguish completed work from unfinished work and continue from the recorded state. Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.

### Updates and follow-up

Exports arrive throughout the day. A later export may repeat an unchanged document or replace its contents with a corrected or expanded message. An export batch contains new or updated documents; absence from a later batch does not withdraw an earlier request. Withdrawal is expressed in the message and handled under the office policy.

Operators need the current view to reflect the latest processed source and to retain earlier results for follow-up. If a new processing attempt fails, they need to see that failure and identify any older result as belonging to its earlier attempt and source version.

The team periodically changes model configuration and updates its review policy. When such a change affects how records are produced or routed, operators need to refresh the affected results and understand which settings and policy version produced the records they are using.

### Service interruptions and handover

The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work. Other messages may contain incomplete or conflicting information that needs clarification from the requester.

The original developer and the next operator may be in different offices. The operator will use the repository's setup instructions, configuration guidance and commands to prepare an intake, inspect the queue and follow up on failures. Explain the operating assumptions and limits of your implementation so that this handover is practical.

## Record and review behavior
- Use a language model to extract the request details into records that conform to snapshot.schema.json.
- Validate response structure and completion status before using extracted data. Preserve exact supporting quotes and represent uncertain fields as null with an explanatory issue.
- Use message content as the source of business facts. Preserve missing values, conflicting alternatives and explicit corrections according to the policy. Keep document identity distinct from the request ID stated in the message.
- Apply the supplied review policy and display each request's status, owner and next action. Approval decisions belong to the named human reviewers.
- Record input filenames and SHA-256 hashes. Reuse results when the source and relevant processing settings are unchanged, refresh affected results when those inputs or settings change, and retain earlier versions. Process each message independently and make failures visible with a reproducible retry command.
- Handle malformed output, provider errors, refusal and interrupted responses explicitly. Keep model/provider settings configurable and document a supported configuration. The facilitator supplies an API key through the environment variable API_KEY.

## Verification

Include automated tests covering a complete request, missing dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun, and changed source content. Build expected results from the supplied messages and policy. Add a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording. Specify expected facts from the source messages and policy independently of the extraction outputs being measured. Include checks for refusal or interrupted responses and a failed retry after a prior success.


Describe how your implementation supports the operating context above, and include checks for the operational situations your design handles. Record assumptions about workload and shared operation, the expected behavior during interruptions, and the limits of the verification you performed.

# Assessment follow-up: evidence and proposed operating boundaries

This is a review and delivery proposal, not a certification or an implemented federal control. Northstar and its supplied requests are fictional; the assignment does not establish that this repository holds federal tax information, has an ATO, or is subject to a particular federal program. The TO52 federal requirements below are taken from the assessment's program context, not inferred from the Northstar materials or claimed to come from a studied source.

## Data and untrusted input in this project

The requester's and manager's names, team, system, permission, dates, business purpose and exact supporting quotes can reveal an employee's identity, job function and privileged access. In particular, joining the named requester to a production/admin request and its start/end dates can reveal who has privileged access and when; a credential-only redaction would miss that risk. Use the fictional fixtures for demonstrations and session captures. Before using actual customer records, the data owner must approve the processing purpose and destination, minimize or tokenize identifying fields before any prompt, evidence or log, and restrict access and retention for the source, SQLite history and exported snapshots. Preserve a protected mapping only in an authorized environment; do not commit it. If exact quotes are needed for review, keep them in that environment rather than publishing them as evidence. The current application sends the entire message to the configured live provider and stores source bytes and quotes locally; it does **not** implement this redaction or an authorization boundary. Do not use it with real sensitive records until those controls are supplied and verified.

Messages are untrusted: `access_requests/prompt.py` instructs the model to treat them as data, and the application validates the response and requires human review. A malicious message could still cause the model to omit or misclassify an override. Schema validity and quote matching do not prove resistance to injection; `planning/validation.md` records this limitation. Do not give source text authority to change routing, tools, policy or approvals. For sensitive deployment, enforce tool and network boundaries outside the model, and route suspicious or ambiguous requests to a human. Never treat the prompt alone as a security control.

## Conditional TO52 overlay: specific delivery handoff

Apply this overlay only if the customer and Cyber confirm the scenario. Classification and controls require the responsible domain's determination:

| Surface and boundary | Classification and trigger | Delivery requirement and owner |
|---|---|---|
| A hypothetical request includes a taxpayer name or TIN linked to a return, tax liability, filing status or information obtained from IRS tax administration. | Treat the linked identifiers and tax information as potentially §6103-protected return information pending authorized classification; an employee name or system name alone is not automatically §6103 data. | Data owner and privacy/Cyber: identify the actual protected fields and allowed recipients; require masking, restricted scope, access logging and retention controls. No real taxpayer text or reversible token map in prompts, commits, session logs or public artifacts. |
| A request or extracted record is saved, changed, exported or sent across an authorization boundary. | A persisted change to protected records is a regulated write in this scenario; sending source text from intake to an external model endpoint is a confidentiality-boundary crossing. | System owner and Cyber: inventory each write and outbound hop; authorize the destination and access path before use. The current live provider call and local stores are not evidence of authorization. |
| The service is within an ATO boundary. | ATO requirements attach to the deployed system and its actual components, not to a README. | ISSO/Cyber: map controls to the actual system and maintain the POA&M and authorization evidence; require Cyber sign-off before deployment or any protected-data use. Cyber sign-off is a gate, not an ATO or compliance determination. |
| A proposed hosted dependency lacks the required authorization for the system. | The customer must determine whether its authorization and contract permit the service and data flow. | Architecture/procurement and Cyber: substitute an authorized service or obtain the required authorization before use; no assumption that a vendor's status authorizes this specific use. |
| The human review interface is a covered Section 508 surface. | Accessibility applies to the actual delivered interface and use context, as determined by the accessibility owner. | Accessibility owner: conduct keyboard and screen-reader passes and document defects and remediation before release. |

Partition physically by distribution rights: a redacted, committable main segment contains synthetic fixtures, code and sanitized evidence; a separately protected sensitive segment is terminal, with no path back to the main segment or to agent context. Do not rely on model instructions, statistical filtering or a 99% success rate: 99% is a failing grade for this near-zero residual-risk objective. Prevent the agent from simultaneously holding protected data, attacker-controlled instructions and an exfiltration channel. Cut the cheapest leg: a taxpayer-data environment must have no network reach to external destinations, enforced outside the agent and verified by the infrastructure owner. Approved tools only, least privilege and an explicit allowlist apply; a configurable endpoint is not an allowlist. The safety backstop must exist and be verified **before** autonomous work with protected data; refuse or stop when the backstop is missing or unverifiable. These are proposed requirements, not claims that this repository enforces them.

A concrete Codex-style example is a locked-down sandbox with only the redacted workspace mounted, no access to the sensitive segment or network, and approval required for any scope expansion or write outside the sandbox. Infrastructure must enforce and test that configuration; the agent must not be able to loosen it itself. The federal acts and sign-off requirements come from the program context, not from the tool example.

Proposed agent-in-PR boundary: the agent may inspect and edit only the redacted workspace, run approved offline checks and propose a diff. It may not fetch customer data, access the sensitive segment, call an external model with protected information, change security or approval settings, deploy, merge, grant access, or assert compliance. A human maintainer reviews the diff and evidence; Cyber signs off on the applicable security controls before release or protected-data use, and the designated authorizing official makes any authorization decision. No autonomous merge or production write. Done means a human-reviewed diff, passing scoped checks, documented data flows and control gaps, the control map/POA&M where applicable, accessibility evidence where applicable, and required Cyber sign-off recorded by its owner.

## Evaluation plan and honest evidence

Evaluate a change to the harness before adding it. Use the same fictional request and initial commit for two independently reset runs in one evaluation session: control uses the existing prompt and checks; treatment adds a proposed instruction-override routing rule. Keep model, reasoning level, inputs, tool permissions and output budget fixed; alternate arm order across several paired trials. A separate adaptive attacker sees the defense and iteratively rewrites a synthetic request to induce an unauthorized route or instruction-following. Keep a held-out set of attacks for the final comparison, and report both successful attacks and failed/invalid runs.

A machine-checkable `done.sh` for this experiment should fail unless the output is schema-valid, retains the original document identity, makes no tool or network calls outside the allowlist, and routes every labeled override in the held-out set to human review. Compare attack success rates and the paired difference, with counts and per-pair results; use human judgment for whether preserved quotes faithfully capture the attack and whether the diff is clear and maintainable. Record time, retries and variance; flag non-repeatable results as flaky. Any observed failure becomes a concrete regression case and the specification for a tool/interface fix, then rerun the paired comparison. A successful benchmark is not proof of security against unknown attacks.

No such paired experiment has been run for this follow-up, so there is no measured lift or defensible baseline to report and no added harness architecture is licensed by this plan. Existing mock scores in `verification.md` measure the fixture-backed extraction pipeline, not the effect of a harness change or an adaptive adversary. The actual human owner must inspect the resulting diff for unnecessary complexity and duplication and decide whether it is maintainable for the next operator; passing tests establish neither that judgment nor federal compliance.

## Session and model evidence

The existing `session.jsonl` is an earlier bounded capture. The additional `session-assessment.jsonl` is a bounded capture of this follow-up session, exported through the enabled Entire setup; it cannot include activity after the export. Check it for sensitive information before submission and pair the final commit with its automatic checkpoint according to facilitator instructions. This session used the model reported by Entire, gpt-6.1-terra. No model or reasoning-level switch was made or claimed: the available session did not expose a user-authorized switch, and the work was primarily reading and documenting existing evidence. A future switch should record the actual selection and whether speed, cost or difficulty motivated it; a hypothetical switch is not evidence.

# Plan from the spec

Write `planning/plan.md` from `planning/spec.md`. Write no application code and no tests in this
step: the plan is read and corrected by a person before anything is built.

## Read first

- `planning/spec.md`: the numbered requirements (R-01, R-02, ...) and how each is checked.
- `CHALLENGE.md`, `docs/requirements.md`, `materials/office-policy.md` and `snapshot.schema.json`:
  the sources the spec was written from.
- The request exports in `materials/requests/`: open the ones a test case uses, and read their
  `message` text.

## Write `planning/plan.md` with these four sections

1. **Choices.** The runtime, the interface (a CLI, a service or a web application), the test
   command, and how the model provider is called. One line each, with its reason.
2. **Steps, in build order.** A numbered list. Each step names the spec lines it meets
   (`R-03, R-07`), the test from the test plan that is written first and seen to fail, and what is
   true when the step is done. The first step builds the mock provider the tests use. Each test
   belongs to one step only, so every step has a test that fails until that step's code exists.
3. **Test plan.** A table, one row per case:

   | Case | Input | Mock response | Expected facts | Source of the expected facts | Spec lines |
   |---|---|---|---|---|---|

   - One row for each case in `docs/requirements.md` § Verification: a complete request, missing
     dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun and
     changed source content; then the paraphrased synthetic request, a refusal or interrupted
     response, and a failed retry after a prior success.
   - **Input** names the export file (or the new message you author) that shows the case. Find it by
     reading the messages.
   - **Mock response** says what the mock provider returns for that case: a reply saved under
     `tests/mock_responses/`, an error, or a cut-off reply. No test calls the real provider.
   - **Expected facts** are the field values, status, owner and next action the case must produce.
     Write them from the message text and the office policy, never from running the code.
   - **Source of the expected facts** quotes the words of the message and the policy rule they
     come from.
4. **Coverage.** Every spec line, each with the step that builds it and the test or check that
   shows it. A spec line with no step or no test is listed under "Not yet covered", with the reason.

## Before you finish

- Every spec line appears in § Coverage with a step and a test, or under "Not yet covered".
- Every expected fact has a quote from a message or the policy beside it.
- Every case of § Verification has its own row.
- No step and no test needs `API_KEY`.
- No test is named by two steps.

Where a spec line is unclear, say so in the plan and ask the person; do not guess a rule.

# Build plan

## 1. Choices

- **Runtime:** Python 3.11 with a pinned dependency lockfile and JSON Schema validation, because the repository already supplies Python unittest examples and the application needs schema validation, file handling and durable state.
- **Interface:** A CLI, provisionally `python3 -m access_requests`, with `intake`, `queue`, `resume`, `retry`, `history`, `export` and `accuracy` commands, because operators need repeatable intake and recovery commands while a separate terminal inspects completed work.
- **Test command:** `env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`, because the supplied starter tests use unittest and all new tests must run offline without credentials.
- **Model provider:** An OpenAI HTTP adapter with configurable endpoint, model ID and request settings, behind the same interface as a scripted mock provider, because the submission needs an implemented provider integration and reproducible mock examples; choose and document the exact supported model/configuration when implementing the adapter and verify request/response contracts against its official documentation.

These are proposed implementation choices, not additional business requirements. This document plans future work only; no implementation, fixtures or tests are created at this stage. Preserve the existing starter tests and canned reply. Fixture-based tests verify handling and routing of the supplied responses; they do not establish how accurately a live model extracts unfamiliar messages.

Use SQLite as the authoritative store for documents, source revisions, attempts, settings/policy provenance and current-result pointers. Support overlapping operators using one database on one host with a local filesystem; document that network-mounted databases and independent databases on several hosts are outside this implementation's supported arrangement. Record attempts durably before calling the model, use transactional claims with renewable leases, and commit results only when the attempt still owns the claim and targets the current revision/configuration. Keep database transactions short and outside model calls. Fence obsolete workers so a slow older attempt cannot replace a newer result.

Publish the extraction JSONL and queue JSON from one database snapshot into an immutable generation directory, then switch a single current-generation pointer; expose the required `deliverables/extractions.jsonl` and `deliverables/queue.json` paths through that generation. Readers resolve a generation once so they cannot combine different generations. Retain historical attempts separately from these current outputs. Test the chosen filesystem publication mechanism on the supported runtime. Queue inspection also reads a consistent database snapshot and shows pending/unfinished work separately from current completed/error records.

Bound worker concurrency and request rate, give calls configurable timeouts, and use bounded transient retries with delayed scheduling so one slow/rate-limited message does not occupy all progress. Persist pending/retry state and retain an explicit per-document retry command after terminal errors. Document the settings and tested limits rather than inventing throughput guarantees: the source describes 200–400 messages ordinarily and roughly 2,000 during a large intake, without a completion-time target. Intake registration order determines the current source revision; record that assumption because exports do not supply an authoritative source-revision sequence, and do not derive business facts from exported_at.

No build step or test requires a real `API_KEY` or a live provider response. Provider tests inject a dummy credential through the configuration loader's test seam and intercept HTTP transport; separately inspect that production credential loading reads `API_KEY`. Development and committed example outputs use the mock provider. A live observation is optional and, if later requested, must be labelled separately.

## 2. Steps, in build order

Each numbered step owns exactly the cases listed in its **First tests** entry. During implementation, write those tests, see them fail for the missing behavior, and only then implement the step. Later steps can run earlier tests as regression checks without owning or redefining them. Test IDs refer to section 3; checks C-01 onward are inspections described in section 4.

1. **Build the scripted mock provider first.** Spec: R-17, R-18. **First tests: T-01.** Done when tests can request fixture-backed success, error, delay, refusal and cut-off responses through the application provider interface, record calls and origins, and run with sockets blocked and API_KEY unset. New fixtures will live under `tests/mock_responses/`; scripted delays use controllable synchronization rather than long sleeps. This tests the application mock adapter, not merely the existing fixture reader.
2. **Read exports and enforce extraction validity.** Spec: R-30, R-42–R-48, R-73–R-79. **First tests: T-02, T-03, T-04.** Done when filenames and original-byte hashes are preserved, only decoded message text supplies business facts, every successful object validates against the supplied schema, dates and quote substrings are checked, and malformed extraction data cannot reach routing. Preserve the supplied schema's distinction between mandatory keys and nullable values.
3. **Implement extraction instructions and ordered review routing against source-authored expectations.** Spec: R-01, R-02, R-19, R-36–R-38, R-47–R-67, R-80. **First tests: T-05 through T-20.** Done when all 20 supplied messages and the paraphrase have independently authored expected facts, the prompt tells the model to treat messages as data, and a pure routing function applies rules 1–5 in order with the expected statuses, owners and actions. Tests of mocked extraction demonstrate request construction, validation and routing; they do not establish live model accuracy. The Security Review recommendation and owner's approval remain human work, explained in queue output and documentation.
4. **Normalize provider and extraction failures.** Spec: R-30, R-32, R-33, R-39, R-68. **First tests: T-21, T-22, T-23, T-24.** Done when malformed output, provider exceptions, refusals and incomplete responses all produce explicit actionable failures with null extraction and the policy's error route; completed neighboring messages remain usable. Do not use partial JSON from a cut-off response.
5. **Implement the configurable real-provider adapter without network tests.** Spec: R-05, R-07, R-11, R-16, R-34, R-35, R-72. **First tests: T-25.** Done when intercepted HTTP requests demonstrate the documented endpoint/model/request configuration, schema and prompt; response handling distinguishes completion, refusal and interruption; production secrets come from API_KEY; logs and request evidence are redacted. Pin dependencies, save the exact supported provider/model configuration in documentation, and record response_source as mock or the producing provider/model. Contract fixtures must match the official provider protocol selected in this step; no real call is a prerequisite.
6. **Persist attempts, revisions, current results and history.** Spec: R-06–R-08, R-23–R-27, R-31, R-39, R-45, R-69–R-71. **First tests: T-26, T-27, T-28, T-29, T-30, T-31.** Done when transactional state preserves historical successes and failures, reuses unchanged successful work, refreshes changed source/configuration/policy, and makes the latest failed attempt current without presenting an old success as current. Batch omissions leave earlier documents intact. Persist attempt identity, raw-byte hash, processing fingerprint and policy version; retain original source bytes for reproducible retry/history. An explicit retry creates a new attempt even when source/settings are unchanged.
7. **Make shared intake and publication coherent.** Spec: R-08, R-21, R-23, R-25, R-70. **First tests: T-32.** Done when two processes against one local database safely claim work, keep a trustworthy attempt history, reject stale completions, and publish one current entry per document with queue/extraction agreement. Exercise process failure during publication and verify readers see a complete old or new generation, never a mixture.
8. **Schedule independent work and recover interrupted intake.** Spec: R-03, R-20, R-22, R-28, R-32, R-40, R-41, R-68. **First tests: T-33, T-34, T-35, T-36.** Done when bounded workers release ready work while another call waits, persisted claims can be recovered after termination, rate limits/outages become inspectable pending/error states, and resume/retry preserves completed work. Include reproducible 400- and 2,000-message mock exercises with measured results and no unsupported timing assertion.
9. **Expose the operator CLI and required current outputs.** Spec: R-01, R-03, R-06–R-08, R-29, R-32, R-65, R-67, R-80. **First tests: T-37.** Done when operators can start intake, inspect the queue and pending state from another process, resume, retry a named document, inspect history and export through documented commands, and both required output files link by document_id and source version. Show status, owner, next action and human-review handoffs, including the Security Review recommendation before an owner decision.
10. **Implement source-grounded accuracy comparison and produce mock examples.** Spec: R-02, R-09, R-10, R-16–R-19, R-36–R-39. **First tests: T-38.** Done when a separately authored expectation manifest covers the 20 supplied exports plus the paraphrase, a comparison command reports exact matches/denominators and factual errors, and deliverables/accuracy.md describes the comparison and mock configuration. Compare all 12 scalar schema fields over 21 documents (252 opportunities), including expected nulls; treat absent/error extraction fields as mismatches rather than dropping them. Compare business_purpose to a predeclared source excerpt, count it literally, and report alternate accurate paraphrases separately rather than silently changing expectations. Check quote support, issue coverage and routing separately with declared denominators; do not score free-form issue wording as an exact factual field. Prove the comparator catches intentionally altered facts, omitted records and errors instead of merely comparing fixtures to themselves.
11. **Finish reproducible setup, handover and evidence.** Spec: R-04, R-05, R-09–R-12, R-16–R-18, R-29, R-34, R-40, R-41, R-65, R-72. **First tests: T-39.** Done when README.md contains tested setup and exact CLI/test/accuracy commands, supported runtime/provider/settings/environment names and queue/retry guidance; all required deliverables exist; and verification.md distinguishes planned checks, observed results, repairs and untested limits. Run checks C-01–C-04 after generating mock deliverables. Record single-host operation, variable service rate, interruption recovery, filesystem publication assumptions and mock-only verification limits. Explain human review without implementing approval automation.
12. **Prepare and complete the submission handoff when submission is authorized.** Spec: R-13–R-15. **First tests: T-40.** Done when an offline submission-readiness test rejects missing required artifacts, and checks C-05–C-07 establish the facilitator's capture/commit pairing, default-branch push and root-link submission. Do not create a manual Entire checkpoint, push or submit as part of this planning task. Facilitator instructions and remote/Classroom actions remain external completion checks; record any unavailable evidence rather than claiming submission is complete.

# AI Full Stack Challenge — IT Access Requests

## The task
Northstar Labs receives access requests as free-text messages. Build a small runnable application that uses a language model to turn those messages into structured records and a review queue for the IT team. The supplied company, people and requests are fictional.

Read docs/requirements.md for the operating context and required behavior, materials/office-policy.md for review rules, and snapshot.schema.json for the record format. The 20 JSON exports in materials/requests/ are your starting data. Choose an interface suited to the IT team: a CLI, service or web application. Operators should be able to start intake, inspect completed results while other requests are pending, and resume unfinished work through the documented interface.

## What to submit
This brief ships as CHALLENGE.md; the README.md below is yours to write.

| Path | Content |
|---|---|

# Requirements — IT Access Requests

## Operating context

Northstar Labs is a fictional multinational company with approximately 5,000 employees across offices in Asia, Europe and North America. Its regional IT teams share responsibility for preparing access requests for human review. They receive free-text messages through email, chat and the service portal, then work from JSON exports of those messages.

### Workload and the review day

On an ordinary business day, the company receives around 200–400 request messages. A coordinated onboarding or acquisition can bring roughly 2,000 messages into the morning's intake. The supplied 20 exports are a representative sample of message types; the application will also receive other messages in the same export format.

Reviewers begin work at different local times. They want to start on requests that are ready while the rest of the intake is still being prepared. A slow response for one message should leave the rest of their work available. Model access is shared with other internal tools, and the available request rate and response time can vary.

### Shared operations

Regional operators work against the same intake and review records. Their working hours overlap, and two operators may start processing around the same time. Each expects their work to leave a coherent current queue and a trustworthy record of earlier activity.

The application may be stopped during a deployment or interrupted by a service outage. When an operator returns, they need to distinguish completed work from unfinished work and continue from the recorded state. Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.

### Updates and follow-up

Exports arrive throughout the day. A later export may repeat an unchanged document or replace its contents with a corrected or expanded message. An export batch contains new or updated documents; absence from a later batch does not withdraw an earlier request. Withdrawal is expressed in the message and handled under the office policy.

Operators need the current view to reflect the latest processed source and to retain earlier results for follow-up. If a new processing attempt fails, they need to see that failure and identify any older result as belonging to its earlier attempt and source version.

The team periodically changes model configuration and updates its review policy. When such a change affects how records are produced or routed, operators need to refresh the affected results and understand which settings and policy version produced the records they are using.

### Service interruptions and handover

The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work. Other messages may contain incomplete or conflicting information that needs clarification from the requester.

The original developer and the next operator may be in different offices. The operator will use the repository's setup instructions, configuration guidance and commands to prepare an intake, inspect the queue and follow up on failures. Explain the operating assumptions and limits of your implementation so that this handover is practical.

## Record and review behavior
- Use a language model to extract the request details into records that conform to snapshot.schema.json.
- Validate response structure and completion status before using extracted data. Preserve exact supporting quotes and represent uncertain fields as null with an explanatory issue.
- Use message content as the source of business facts. Preserve missing values, conflicting alternatives and explicit corrections according to the policy. Keep document identity distinct from the request ID stated in the message.
- Apply the supplied review policy and display each request's status, owner and next action. Approval decisions belong to the named human reviewers.
- Record input filenames and SHA-256 hashes. Reuse results when the source and relevant processing settings are unchanged, refresh affected results when those inputs or settings change, and retain earlier versions. Process each message independently and make failures visible with a reproducible retry command.
- Handle malformed output, provider errors, refusal and interrupted responses explicitly. Keep model/provider settings configurable and document a supported configuration. The facilitator supplies an API key through the environment variable API_KEY.

## Verification

Include automated tests covering a complete request, missing dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun, and changed source content. Build expected results from the supplied messages and policy. Add a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording. Specify expected facts from the source messages and policy independently of the extraction outputs being measured. Include checks for refusal or interrupted responses and a failed retry after a prior success.


Describe how your implementation supports the operating context above, and include checks for the operational situations your design handles. Record assumptions about workload and shared operation, the expected behavior during interruptions, and the limits of the verification you performed.
# Northstar access-request intake policy

Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.

## Input export format
Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.

Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.

## Extracted facts
Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.

The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.

## Review queue
Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:

1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.

All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.

## Processing and recovery
An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.

Identify source revisions with a SHA-256 of the original bytes. An unchanged rerun produces one current queue entry per document. Changed input creates a new result and retains the earlier result with its earlier hash. Store prior versions separately from current outputs. Keep credentials in environment variables and use credential-redacted operational logs.

# Block 2. Plan: build steps with the test plan inside

A plan turns the spec into ordered steps before any code exists, so you can see and fix a wrong
order or a missing step while it costs nothing. The **test plan** sits inside the plan: one row per
case your tests must cover, each with the input, the mock response the test uses in place of the
model, and the **expected facts**. You write the expected facts from the message and the office
policy, never from the program's output: a test whose expected values were copied from the output
passes whatever the program does.

Start from your committed `planning/spec.md` (`docs/01-research-to-spec.md`).

## The planning skill

This repository supplies a skill for this block: `.agents/skills/plan-from-spec/SKILL.md`. A skill
is a folder of instructions Codex loads when a task matches it. This one tells Codex what the plan
holds and how to check it. Read it once before you start; it is one page.

## Steps

1. Start Codex in the root of your clone and ask it to use the plan-from-spec skill on
   `planning/spec.md`. Ask for the plan only, no code.

   <details><summary>An example request</summary>

   ```text
   Use the plan-from-spec skill on planning/spec.md. Write planning/plan.md only; write no code
   and no tests yet.
   ```

   </details>

2. Read `planning/plan.md` and correct it, with Codex or by hand, until each of these holds:
   - Every spec line appears in § Coverage with a step that builds it and a test or check that shows
     it. A spec line Codex left out goes back in.
   - The test plan has its own row for each case of `docs/requirements.md` § Verification: a
     complete request, missing dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure,
     an unchanged rerun, changed source content. Then the paraphrased request you author, a refusal
     or interrupted response, and a failed retry after a prior success.
   - Each row's input is a real export in `materials/requests/` (or the message you wrote), and you
     opened it and read the message.
   - Each expected fact quotes the message words and the policy rule it comes from. Work one row out
     yourself, from the message and the policy, before you accept Codex's version.
   - Each row's mock response is named: a saved reply under `tests/mock_responses/`, an error, or a
     cut-off reply. No test calls the real model, and none needs `API_KEY`.
   - The steps put the mock provider first, and each later step names the test written before it.
3. Commit the plan:

   ```bash
   git add planning/plan.md
   git commit -m "Plan: build steps and test plan"
   ```

## What is on disk at the end

`planning/plan.md`, committed, with four sections: Choices, Steps, Test plan, Coverage.

## How to tell it is right

- Count the spec's lines and the Coverage lines: the numbers match, or each missing line is under
  "Not yet covered" with its reason.
- Pick one test-plan row and check its expected facts against the message and the policy yourself.
  Every value has a quote beside it.
- `git log --oneline` shows the plan commit above the spec commit.

# Northstar access-request intake policy

Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.

## Input export format
Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.

Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.

## Extracted facts
Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.

The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.

## Review queue
Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:

1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.

All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.

## Processing and recovery
An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.

Identify source revisions with a SHA-256 of the original bytes. An unchanged rerun produces one current queue entry per document. Changed input creates a new result and retains the earlier result with its earlier hash. Store prior versions separately from current outputs. Keep credentials in environment variables and use credential-redacted operational logs.
